passage: The waiting room outside the college sports physio smelled of antiseptic and old mats. Leela sat with her knee strapped, staring at the trophy cabinet. Two months ago she'd been picked for the state hockey camp, the first step toward the national team she'd trained for since she was twelve. Then the tackle. The torn ligament. The doctor's words that morning had been careful and kind: she'd walk and run again, but competitive hockey at that level probably wasn't coming back. Her teammate Gopika came in, sat down, and handed her a bottle of water. Leela said, "I don't even know who I am if I'm not that." Gopika didn't try to fix it. She just said, "You're still you," and stayed until the physio called her name.

qa.q: Where did Leela sit with her knee strapped?
qa.a: In the waiting room outside the college sports physio.

qa.q: What does Leela mean when she says she doesn't know who she is anymore?
qa.a: She is grieving not just the injury but the future and identity she had built around hockey since she was twelve.

qa.q: Why was Gopika's quiet presence helpful?
qa.a: She didn't rush to fix or minimise the loss, which let Leela feel her sorrow without being alone. 🤍

qa.q: How might the loss feel different for Gopika, who is still on the team?
qa.a: She may feel sad for her friend and perhaps a little guilty that her own path continues while Leela's has changed.

grounding: Shows a young adult grieving the loss of an idealised future after a career-ending injury.

passage:
Dear Bhaiya,

You asked why I've been quiet on calls. Meera and I broke up. Four years. It was mutual, which somehow makes it worse. Nobody did anything wrong. We just wanted different cities, different lives.

I keep reaching for my phone to tell her small things, like the new chai place near the office, and then I remember. I walk past our bench in the park and feel hollow. I had a whole future in my head: the flat, the dog, Sunday lunches with both families. Now that future is just gone, and I didn't know you could grieve something that never actually happened.

I'm okay, mostly. Going to work, eating. Just sad in a deep, slow way.

Come home for Diwali?

Tanvir

qa.q: How long were Tanvir and Meera together?
qa.a: Four years.

qa.q: Why does Tanvir feel the grief is for more than Meera herself?
qa.a: Tanvir is mourning the imagined future they had planned together, the flat, the dog, the family lunches, which now won't happen.

qa.q: What could Bhaiya do in reply?
qa.a: Call Tanvir, listen without trying to fix it, and make a plan to be together at Diwali as Tanvir asked. 🫂

qa.q: How might Meera be experiencing the same breakup?
qa.a: Since it was mutual, she may also be grieving the future they shared, even though she agreed it had to end.

grounding: A young adult writes about the deep sorrow of losing a long relationship and the future they had imagined.

passage: Dhruv rubbed his face with both hands. "Amandeep, you know how long I prepared for the army. Since Class 9. Morning runs, pushups on the terrace, the medical, the written test, the interview. I thought I'd done well. Yesterday the final list came out. My name wasn't there. And I'm over the age limit for trying again. That's it. Done. I didn't cry in front of Mummy. I went to the ground where I used to run and sat there till it got dark. It's not just the job, you know? It's the picture I carried of myself in uniform, making Papa proud. That picture's just... gone. I don't know what I want now. I'm not asking you to fix it. I just needed to say it out loud to someone."

qa.q: Since which class had Dhruv been preparing for the army?
qa.a: Since Class 9.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv go to the ground and sit there until dark?
qa.a: He was grieving deeply and needed a place to feel the loss privately, away from his mother.

qa.q: How could Amandeep best respond right now?
qa.a: By listening and staying with him instead of offering quick solutions, as Dhruv asked, and checking in over the next days.

qa.q: What would change if Dhruv's father were in the room hearing this?
qa.a: Dhruv might feel he had failed him, or he might realise his father cares about him more than the uniform.

grounding: A young man tells a friend about the sorrow of losing the future he had long imagined for himself.

passage: I'm Omkar, Maria's younger brother. Last month her engagement to the man she'd been with since college ended. Five years. She didn't explain much to us, only that it was over and nobody did anything terrible. At first she kept going to work like normal. Then I noticed she'd stopped singing in the shower, which she has done my whole life. On Sunday she sat on the balcony with the box of wedding cards they had already printed and folded them into little boats, one by one, without speaking. I sat with her. I don't know if she was angry or just very sad. When the box was empty, she said, 'I had the whole house planned. Even the curtains.' Then she went in and made us both tea.

qa.q: How long had Maria been with the man?
qa.a: Five years, since college.

qa.q: What might folding the wedding cards into boats suggest about Maria's feelings?
qa.a: It may suggest she was quietly grieving the future she had planned and letting it go slowly, though Omkar can't be sure.

qa.q: How could Omkar keep supporting his sister?
qa.a: He can keep sitting with her without pushing for explanations, and if the sadness stays heavy, gently suggest family time or a counsellor.

qa.q: How might this loss feel different for Maria than for her family?
qa.a: For her it is the loss of a whole imagined life, down to the curtains; the family sees the breakup but not all the plans that ended with it.

grounding: Shows a young adult grieving the end of a long relationship and the future she had imagined, seen by her brother.

passage:
Week one: The doctor's words were gentle, but Jomon, twenty-one, heard only that he would never play at that level again. At home he turned his team jersey inside out and stuffed it at the back of the cupboard. When Ishita called, he said he was fine and hung up.
Week three: Ishita came anyway, with banana chips. He talked for an hour about the trials he'd miss, the coach who had believed in him, the future he had drawn since he was twelve. He cried, which he hadn't done in years. She just listened.
Week six: He went to the ground as a spectator for the first time. It hurt to watch. On the way out he asked the junior coach if they needed help with the under-twelves.

qa.q: What did Jomon do with his team jersey?
qa.a: He turned it inside out and stuffed it at the back of the cupboard.

qa.q: Why did Jomon tell Ishita he was fine and hang up in week one?
qa.a: He was too raw with grief to talk and wanted to shut out the loss of his future.

qa.q: What helped Jomon move from hiding to grieving?
qa.a: Ishita coming anyway and listening without trying to fix things gave him space to cry and talk.

qa.q: How might the under-twelves be affected if Jomon helps coach?
qa.a: They would gain a skilled, dedicated coach who knows the game deeply.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult processing the loss of an idealised sporting future over several weeks.

passage: "Tejas, you think this pain will never end? When I, your Manoj Chacha, was twenty-two, I'd prepared for the civil services exam for four years. Everyone in our family believed I'd be an officer. I failed the final interview twice. The second time, I sat on the steps of the exam centre in Delhi until it was dark. It wasn't just the exam. It was the whole life I'd imagined: the uniform, my mother's pride. That life died that day. I grieved it for a year. Then I took a teaching job, just to survive. Now I've taught for thirty years, and some of my students became officers."

qa.q: How many times did young Manoj fail the final interview?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: What was young Manoj feeling on the steps of the exam centre?
qa.a: He felt deep sorrow, grieving the whole future he had imagined.

qa.q: What turning point in the story began Manoj's new path?
qa.a: Taking a teaching job after a year of grief, which became his life's work.

qa.q: How might Manoj's mother have felt about his failure?
qa.a: Probably sad for him too, though she may later have been proud of his teaching.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how as a young adult he grieved the loss of an idealised future.

passage: After five years together, Leela, twenty-two, and her partner had ended it, and she had one rainy Sunday to move out of their shared flat. Her friend Ganga came with a borrowed car. They carried boxes down four flights in the downpour. Leela kept stopping: at the mug they'd bought in Goa, at the plant they'd named. Ganga didn't hurry her. In the car, soaked, Leela finally said, "It's not just him. It's every plan we made. The house, the dog, all of it." Ganga held her hand. "Then grieve all of it. We'll go slow."

qa.q: How many flights of stairs did they carry boxes down?
qa.a: Four flights.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling when she stopped at the mug and the plant?
qa.a: She was grieving and heartbroken, for the relationship and for all the future plans that ended with it.

qa.q: What did Ganga do that helped?
qa.a: She stayed patient, didn't rush Leela and let her grieve the whole loss.

qa.q: What is it like for Ganga on that rainy moving day?
qa.a: Tiring and sad, but she chooses to be steady for her friend.

grounding: Shows a young adult grieving the end of a long relationship and the future it held, with a friend's support.

passage: Vasudha, twenty, had danced since she was six. The knee injury came in the final year of college, and the doctor was clear: no professional dancing. For weeks she couldn't even look at her ghungroos. Her friend Zainab visited every Sunday in their Pune hostel and didn't talk about dance unless Vasudha did. One evening Vasudha opened her cupboard, held the ghungroos and cried until her chest hurt. "I didn't just lose dancing," she said. "I lost the person I was going to be." Zainab sat beside her. "You're still her. Just on a different road." Vasudha didn't believe it yet, but she didn't put the ghungroos away.

qa.q: When did Vasudha start dancing?
qa.a: When she was six.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling as she held the ghungroos?
qa.a: She was heartbroken, grieving the future she had imagined as a dancer.

qa.q: What did Zainab do that helped?
qa.a: She visited regularly, followed Vasudha's lead on talking about dance and offered gentle hope.

qa.q: How might Zainab feel watching Vasudha cry?
qa.a: Sad for her friend and wanting to support her without rushing her.

grounding: Shows a young adult grieving the loss of an idealised future after an injury, with a friend's support.

passage:
"Lakshmi, you haven't touched your tea."
"I'm fine, Irfan."
"You're not."
She put the cup down. "Five years. We were going to move to Chennai together. We'd picked names for a dog we never got."
"I know."
"And he just said, 'I think we want different lives.' Like it was a weather report."
Irfan was quiet.
"It's not just him I lost. It's the whole future. The flat, the Sunday mornings, all of it. I planned my life around it."
"You're allowed to grieve all of that."
Lakshmi's voice cracked. "I keep waking up and forgetting, and then remembering."
Irfan slid the tea closer. "Drink. I'm not going anywhere tonight."
She held the cup with both hands. "Thank you."

qa.q: How long had Lakshmi's relationship lasted?
qa.a: Five years.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling when her voice cracked?
qa.a: She felt deep sorrow and grief, not just for the person but for the whole future she had planned.

qa.q: What did Irfan do that helped Lakshmi?
qa.a: Irfan listened quietly, said she was allowed to grieve, and stayed with her.

qa.q: What is it like for Irfan to sit with Lakshmi's grief?
qa.a: Irfan seems steady and caring, willing to stay with her pain without trying to fix it.

grounding: A young woman grieves the end of a five-year relationship and the future she had imagined, with a friend's support.

passage: I'm Indu. For three years, I tried to get into medical college. Three attempts at the entrance exam. The third time, I missed the cut-off by eleven marks. I didn't cry that day. I cleaned my whole room instead. The crying came a week later, when I saw my old white coat from the school science fair. I'd imagined myself as a doctor since I was nine. That version of me was gone. My father, Anand, sat with me that night. He didn't tell me to try again or to move on. He just said, "You worked so hard. It's okay to be sad about this." I'm in a biotechnology course now. Some days I like it. Some days I still miss the doctor I was going to be.

qa.q: By how many marks did Indu miss the cut-off the third time?
qa.a: By eleven marks.

qa.q: How did Indu feel when seeing the old white coat?
qa.a: Indu felt deep sorrow, grieving the future self imagined since childhood.

qa.q: What did Anand do that helped Indu grieve?
qa.a: He sat with Indu and acknowledged the hard work, saying it was okay to be sad, without pushing to move on.

qa.q: How might Anand have felt watching Indu's disappointment?
qa.a: He likely felt sad and protective, sharing in the grief.

grounding: A young adult reflects on grieving the loss of an imagined future as a doctor after missing the entrance cut-off.

passage:
College counsellor's note. Kavitha Rao. Monday.
Abhinav, third-year, came in after the sports doctor told him his knee injury means he can't play competitive cricket again. He spoke flatly at first, listing facts. Then he said, "I was going to try for the state team next year. That was my whole plan." He stopped and put his face in his hands for a long time. I didn't rush him. When he looked up, he said he didn't know who he was without cricket. I told him that this loss is real and deserves grieving, not just "moving on." We talked about people who could be with him this week. He agreed to call his older brother tonight. We will meet again on Thursday.

qa.q: What does Abhinav's knee injury mean for him?
qa.a: He can't play competitive cricket again.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling when he put his face in his hands?
qa.a: He felt grief and deep sorrow for the future he had planned, and lost about who he was.

qa.q: What did Kavitha Rao do that helped?
qa.a: She gave him time without rushing, named the loss as real, and made sure he would call his brother that night.

qa.q: How might Abhinav's older brother feel receiving the call?
qa.a: He may feel sad for Abhinav and glad he reached out.

grounding: A counsellor records a young man grieving the loss of his cricket career and planned future.

passage:
Tuesday night
Reena and I broke up four months ago. I thought I was done being sad. Today I found her handwriting on a grocery list in my old notebook, "eggs, bread, dhaniya," and I sat on the floor of my room for an hour.
It's not only her. It's the whole future I'd built in my head. The flat we talked about, the dog, her mother's Sunday lunches. I'm grieving a life that didn't happen.
Nobody warns you that it comes back like this, from a list.
I called my brother. He didn't say "move on." He just stayed on the phone while I cried.
I'm not throwing the list away. Not yet.
Amandeep

qa.q: What was on Reena's grocery list?
qa.a: Eggs, bread, dhaniya.

qa.q: What is Amandeep feeling after finding the list?
qa.a: Amandeep feels a deep sorrow and grief, not only for Reena but for the future imagined together.

qa.q: What helped Amandeep tonight, and what could help next?
qa.a: Calling the brother who just stayed on the line helped; keeping close to people and, if the sadness keeps weighing heavily, talking to a counsellor could help too.

qa.q: How might Amandeep's brother feel after that phone call?
qa.a: He may feel sad for his sibling and glad he could simply be there.

grounding: A young adult's diary processing the loss of a long relationship and an imagined future.

passage:
In the small town where Trisha grew up, everyone knew she'd marry Rohit. They'd been together since school. Last month he told her he'd accepted a job abroad and wanted to go alone.
Trisha kept working at her father's cloth shop. She measured, cut, smiled at customers. At night she lay awake remembering the house they had planned near the temple tank.
Her friend Aparna came to the shop on Friday with two cups of tea and sat on the stool behind the counter.
"You don't have to smile at me," Aparna said.
Trisha folded a piece of cotton very carefully. Then she put her face in it and cried.
Aparna rubbed her back. "It's a real loss. The whole future, not just him."
Trisha nodded into the cloth.

qa.q: Where did Trisha work after the breakup?
qa.a: At her father's cloth shop.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling as she kept working?
qa.a: She felt deep sorrow and grief, hiding it behind smiles and lying awake at night.

qa.q: How did Aparna help in a way that worked?
qa.a: She came with tea, told Trisha she didn't have to smile, and named the loss as real.

qa.q: How might Trisha's father see her in these weeks?
qa.a: He may notice she is working hard but quiet, and feel worried for her.

grounding: Shows a young adult grieving the end of a long relationship and imagined future in a small town.

passage: The apartment in Lisbon still had two coffee cups in the drying rack when Rania came back from the station. Tomás had taken the rest of his things that morning, after four years, and after all the evenings they'd spent planning the flat in Porto they would never rent. She sat on the kitchen floor with his cup in her hands and didn't cry for a long time. Then she did, for an hour. Her friend Ines arrived with soup and didn't ask questions. Later Rania said, "It isn't only him I'm missing. It's the whole life I'd already moved into in my head." Ines nodded and stayed the night on the sofa. In the morning Rania put one cup away.

qa.q: How long had Rania and Tomás been together?
qa.a: Four years.

qa.q: What does Rania mean by missing "the whole life I'd already moved into in my head"?
qa.a: She is grieving not just Tomás but the future they planned in Porto, a deep sorrow for an imagined life that is now gone.

qa.q: What helped Rania through the first night?
qa.a: Letting herself cry, and having Ines there with soup and no questions, gave her room to grieve without being alone.

qa.q: What is it like for Ines to stay the night?
qa.a: Ines probably feels sad for Rania and chooses quiet presence over advice, which seems to be what Rania needs.

grounding: Shows a young adult grieving both a long relationship and the future she had imagined with him.
